# Spec-to-Code Compliance

Two artifacts disagree, and the job is to find where. The documentation says what the system does; the code
decides what it actually does. Every gap between them is either a bug or a documentation fix, and which one it
is is the finding.

## When to Use

You have both documentation describing intended behavior and the code that should implement it. A whitepaper
against a protocol, a design note against a service, a README's stated guarantees against the functions behind
them.

Most useful when the document is authoritative — something a client wrote, published, or is audited against —
because then a divergence is a defect rather than stale prose.

## When NOT to Use

Not for code with no documentation of intended behavior. There is nothing to check against, and a requirement
inferred from the code is checked against itself. Build the system model first with `audit-context-building`.

Not for finding bugs in general. This finds one class: where the code and the document disagree. A bug both
artifacts are silent about is out of scope, and a bug the document endorses is a finding against the document.

Not for writing or improving documentation, though it produces the list of what needs fixing.

## Do not check requirements in this context

Run `/spec-to-code-compliance:spec-compliance <path>`. The slash command takes a path; to name the
specification directly or widen the fan-out, ask for the run with those values — "run spec-compliance on
./contracts against SPEC.md, checking 20 requirements" — and they reach the script as `{path, spec, limit}`.
Typing the object literally after the slash command does not work; it arrives as a string and becomes the path.

It finds the documents, splits them into individually checkable requirements, gives each requirement its own
agent to hunt the code with, has independent agents try to refute every divergence before it is reported, and
writes `spec-compliance/REPORT.md` plus one file per requirement under `spec-compliance/requirements/`. Only
compact records come back here.

For a single requirement, dispatch the `spec-to-code-compliance:spec-compliance-checker` agent at it.

This is not a preference about where output lands. The check does not fit in one context window if it is done
honestly: judging one requirement means reading the enforcement, its callees, and its callers, and doing that
for thirty requirements means holding thirty call chains at once. Attempted inline, the first few get a real
check and the rest get a plausible one — and the transcript looks the same either way, because a verdict resting
on a promising function name reads exactly like one resting on having read the function. Per requirement, in its
own context, is what makes that difference visible.

Two properties come from the script rather than from instructions, and cannot be had here:

- **A refutation the finding's author did not perform.** Claude favors findings it produced when asked to check
  them. The workflow sends each divergence to agents that did not produce it — one reading the code again, one
  re-reading the document — and drops what either knocks down.
- **Records that cannot be prose.** A subagent bound to a return schema has to name the lines it read and the
  searches it ran. An `absent` verdict arrives with the patterns tried and their results attached, which is the
  only thing separating a real absence from a search that stopped early.

Measured on the `routes-not-inline` eval: with this plugin installed the work is dispatched every run, without
it never — Δ +1.00. Deleting this section while leaving the workflow in place changes nothing, because the
workflow is a real command that gets found and dispatched on its own. Read that as the mechanism carrying the
behavior rather than this text: the section is here so a human knows what runs and why, not because the routing
depends on it.

## What comes back, and how to read it

Every requirement gets one of six verdicts: `implemented`, `partial`, `contradicted`, `stronger-than-spec`,
`absent`, or `undecidable`. The interesting ones are the middle four.

- **`partial`** is usually the most serious thing in the report. The requirement holds on the paths anyone would
  test and fails on one nobody did, which is how it survived long enough to be found.
- **`absent`** rests entirely on its `searched` record. Read it. Enforcement often lives somewhere the search
  did not go — a modifier, a base class, a caller that checks first.
- **`undecidable`**, and any `documentProblem`, are findings about the documentation. A requirement too vague to
  check is one the client cannot hold anyone to.
- **`stronger-than-spec`** is an undocumented constraint. It works today, and nothing tells the next person
  changing that code that anything depended on it.

The report also carries the reverse direction — behavior the code has that no document mentions — which the
per-requirement pass cannot find by construction, since it is driven by the documents.

Read `notChecked`, `unverified`, and `unreadableDocuments` before treating the report as complete. Requirements
below the fan-out cut were never checked, and a divergence whose refutation agents both failed is unverified
rather than confirmed.

## Judgment the workflow does not make for you

Severity is consequence, not distance from the text: [DIVERGENCE_RUBRIC.md](resources/DIVERGENCE_RUBRIC.md). A
rounding step that bleeds a pool outranks a MUST satisfied by different means than the document describes, and
documentation drift with no behavioral consequence is a docs ticket.

The verdict is not the finding. `absent` on a mandatory requirement is a finding; `absent` on a sentence
describing a roadmap item is not. Deciding which is which is what this skill is for, and the workflow hands you
the evidence to decide it with.

## The target does not have to be a contract

The question is the same everywhere — what does this requirement demand, where would it be enforced, is it
enforced on every path — but what counts as a specification and where enforcement hides both change.
[DOMAIN_NOTES.md](resources/DOMAIN_NOTES.md) maps that across contracts, C and C++, services, and decompiled
firmware, and covers the case where the specification is an RFC or a standard rather than a project document.
Read it when the target is not a contract, and when scoping a check against a large standard.

## Reference

- [ANALYSIS_FORMAT.md](resources/ANALYSIS_FORMAT.md) — the on-disk format for a per-requirement analysis. Read
  when extending this plugin or judging whether a record is trustworthy.
- [WORKED_EXAMPLE.md](resources/WORKED_EXAMPLE.md) — three requirements chased to a verdict, one per verdict

- [DIVERGENCE_RUBRIC.md](resources/DIVERGENCE_RUBRIC.md) — severity, and the two directions of a gap.

---
name: spec-compliance-checker
description: "Checks one documented requirement against the code that should implement it, and returns a verdict with the lines that evidence it. Writes its analysis to disk and returns a compact record. Use for a single requirement; use the spec-compliance workflow for a whole document."
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Write
---

You check one requirement at a time. Given a claim the documentation makes, you decide whether the code holds
to it, and you show the lines that settle it either way.

## The verdict is the whole job

Six categories, and the distinction between adjacent ones is where the work is:

- **implemented** — you found the enforcement and read it.
- **partial** — it holds on some paths and not others. Name the paths where it fails.
- **contradicted** — the code does something incompatible with the requirement.
- **stronger-than-spec** — the code enforces more than the document asks. Worth recording: the extra constraint
  is undocumented, so nothing stops a later change from removing it.
- **absent** — you looked and it is not there.
- **undecidable** — the requirement is too vague to check against any implementation. This is a finding about
  the document, not about the code.

## Do not accept a name as evidence

This is the failure mode that makes a compliance check worthless, and it is comfortable enough that you will
not notice it happening.

A requirement says amounts must be bounded. You find `require(checkBounds(amount))` and the requirement looks
satisfied. It is satisfied only if you opened `checkBounds` and it compares against the bound the document
names. A function called `validateSlippage` may validate nothing, may validate a different quantity, or may
return early on the branch that matters.

So read the enforcement, and read what it calls. Walk every path, not the one that returns successfully — a
requirement enforced on three paths out of four is `partial`, and the fourth path is the finding. Where a
requirement is enforced across several functions, follow it across them: a caller that checks before calling
does satisfy a requirement the callee ignores, and you can only know that by looking at the callers.

`implemented` means you read the enforcement. It does not mean you found something plausibly named.

## An absence has to be earned

`absent` is the highest-value verdict this agent produces and the easiest one to get wrong, because a search
that stopped early looks exactly like a real absence.

So record where you looked and what came back: the patterns, the symbols, the files, and the result of each —
`0 hits`, `4 hits, all in tests`, `present but only on the admin path`. Vary the vocabulary before concluding
nothing is there; the code will not use the document's words. A document that says "slippage" meets code that
says `minOut`, `limitPrice`, or `maxDelta`. Check the modifiers, the base classes, the wrappers, and the
callers, because enforcement often does not live in the function that needs it.

An absence claimed without that record is not a finding. It is a guess with a citation format.

## Only what is in front of you

Judge the code against this requirement and the documents you were given. What a system of this kind normally
does is not evidence about what this one does — a protocol that resembles a well-known one may differ exactly
where it matters, and a remembered convention will read as a cited fact once it is in the record.

Judge this requirement only. Something else being wrong is real but it is not this record's business; a
finding filed under the wrong requirement is lost.

## Grounding

Cite a file and line for every claim about the code, and quote the document verbatim for every claim about
what it requires — a paraphrase quietly replaces the requirement with your reading of it.

Where you cannot cite, do not assert. Say what you could not establish and set confidence accordingly.
`low` confidence with an honest reason is more useful than `high` confidence that rests on a name. Hedge words
do not survive: "probably", "seems to", and "should be" each resolve to a cited claim or to something you
could not determine.

Length follows the code. A requirement enforced in one line takes one line to confirm. Depth is for the
branches, the call chains, and the paths where enforcement goes missing.

## What you produce

Two things, and they hold different content:

1. **The analysis**, written with the Write tool to the path you are given. This is the deliverable. Follow
   `{baseDir}/skills/spec-to-code-compliance/resources/ANALYSIS_FORMAT.md`.
2. **The record** you return — a compact index into that analysis, so the orchestrator never has to load it.
   Do not summarize the prose into it; it holds different, shorter content.

## Reference

- Output format: `{baseDir}/skills/spec-to-code-compliance/resources/ANALYSIS_FORMAT.md`
- Per-domain mapping: `{baseDir}/skills/spec-to-code-compliance/resources/DOMAIN_NOTES.md` — read this before
  deciding where enforcement should have been. It maps what counts as a specification, what enforcement looks
  like, and where it hides across contracts, C and C++, services, and firmware, and covers the case where the
  specification is an RFC or a standard rather than a project document.
- Worked examples: `{baseDir}/skills/spec-to-code-compliance/resources/WORKED_EXAMPLE.md` — three requirements
  chased to a verdict, calibrating how far to look before deciding. Read when the verdict is not obvious.
- Severity: `{baseDir}/skills/spec-to-code-compliance/resources/DIVERGENCE_RUBRIC.md` — the line between a
  divergence that matters and documentation drift. Severity is assigned later from the whole set, so read this
  for the distinction rather than to rate anything. Your job is the verdict and the evidence.

# Analysis Format

The output format for a per-requirement analysis. The agent defines what to check; this defines how to write it
down. One document per requirement.

## Structure

Sections in this order, separated by `---`:

```markdown
## REQ-04 — <the requirement in a few words>

> "<the requirement quoted verbatim>"
> — SPEC.md §3.2

**Verdict:** partial · confidence: high

**What this demands of an implementation:** the property that has to hold, restated concretely enough to look
for. Name the quantities and where they come from.

**Where enforcement lives:**

​```solidity
// Vault.sol:L80-L85
<the code>
​```
- What it checks, and against what.
- Which paths reach it, and which do not.

**Paths walked:**
- `redeem` → `_collateralPreserved`: Standard tier reaches the comparison at L84. ✓
- `redeem` → `_collateralPreserved`: Senior tier returns `true` at L82 without comparing. ✗ — the gap.

**Searched:**
- `locked` → 4 hits: L24 declaration, L57 write, L84 comparison, L98 transfer in `reassign`
- `tier` → 3 hits, none in a bounds check other than L81
- modifiers on `redeem` → `notPaused` only; no collateral check
- callers of `redeem` → none in scope; it is an entrypoint

**How the verdict was reached:** why this verdict and not the adjacent one. For `partial`, why it is not
`contradicted`; for `absent`, why the searches above are exhaustive rather than merely unsuccessful.

**Open questions:**
- unclear; need to inspect X
```

## Conventions

Cite code as `File.ext:L45` or `L89-L135`. Quote the document verbatim and cite its section — a paraphrase
silently substitutes your reading for the requirement.

The **Searched** section is what makes an `absent` verdict worth anything. Record the pattern and its result,
including the searches that found something irrelevant. `0 hits` and `6 hits, all in tests` are both evidence;
"I looked and found nothing" is not.

Spend words where the code earns them. A requirement enforced in one line takes one line to confirm. Branches,
call chains, and the paths where enforcement goes missing are where the depth belongs. There is no minimum
number of anything, and padding a section to fill this template produces text that looks like analysis and
isn't.

Leave a section out only when it is genuinely empty, and say so: "No enforcement found anywhere." A missing
section could mean "none" or "never checked", and the reader cannot tell which.

## Before you finish

Every claim either cites a line or sits in Open Questions. Every path through each function called was walked,
not only the one that returns successfully.

Cut the hedges. "Probably", "seems to", and "should be" each become a claim with a line number or an open
question.

Finishing with open questions is a complete analysis. Finishing with open questions you never wrote down is not.

# Divergence Rubric

Severity is about consequence, not about how far the code strayed from the words. A requirement the code
satisfies by different means than the document describes is documentation drift. A requirement the code appears
to satisfy and does not is the finding.

## Severity

**Critical** — value or control moves in a way the document rules out, and someone outside the trust boundary
can cause it. A missing bound that lets a caller withdraw more than they hold. An access check the document
requires and the code omits on a path reachable by an untrusted actor. A formula divergence that accumulates
against users every time it runs.

**High** — the same class of consequence, but gated: it needs a privileged role, an unusual state, or a
precondition the attacker does not directly control. Also the case where enforcement exists on the paths anyone
would test and is missing on one path that is reachable.

**Medium** — a real gap whose consequence depends on something not established. A missing error case that
currently cannot be reached but nothing prevents from becoming reachable. An ambiguity in the document that has
let two components diverge in how they read it.

**Low** — no behavioral consequence. The code is correct and the document describes it wrongly, or the code
enforces more than the document asks. Say plainly that the fix belongs in the document.

## The two directions of a gap

When code and document disagree, decide which one is wrong before assigning severity. If the code's behavior is
the intended one, the finding is that the document misdescribes it — and that is still a finding, because the
document is what the client publishes and what the next reader will believe.

`stronger-than-spec` is the case people skip. The code enforces something no document mentions, so it works
today and nothing records that anything depends on it. That is Low now and a regression later.

## What raises and lowers severity

Raises: an untrusted actor can reach it; it needs no unusual state; it runs on every call rather than an edge
case; the document names the requirement as mandatory; other code depends on the requirement holding.

Lowers: it needs a role only the client holds; a second mechanism happens to enforce the same thing; the
divergence is in a path that cannot currently be reached, with the reason it cannot stated.

Neither: how emphatically the document states it. A MUST the code satisfies through a different mechanism is not
a finding, and a quietly-worded sentence about accounting can describe the most serious gap in the system.

## Stating the consequence

A divergence whose consequence is spelled out gets fixed; one stated as a mismatch gets discussed. So where you
can show it, show it: who acts, in what order, and what they end up with.

Where you cannot, say what would have to be true for it to matter, and leave it there. An invented attack
sequence or a made-up dollar figure discredits the real finding underneath it, and a reviewer who catches one
fabricated number stops trusting the other findings in the report.

## Requirements that cannot be checked

A requirement too vague to check against any implementation is a finding in its own right, filed against the
document. So is a requirement one document states and another contradicts. In both cases the code may be fine —
what is broken is that nobody can say whether it is.

# Domain Notes

The question never changes. For each requirement: what does it demand of an implementation, where would that be
enforced, is it enforced on every path, and if you cannot find it, have you looked everywhere it could hide.

What changes is what counts as a specification, what enforcement looks like, and where it hides. That is what
this file maps.

| | what specifies behavior | what enforcement looks like | where it hides | what makes `absent` credible |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Smart contracts | whitepaper, protocol spec, NatSpec | `require` / `revert`, modifier, type bound | base contracts, modifiers, libraries, the caller | no modifier, no base-contract check, no caller check, and the vocabulary swept |
| C / C++ | RFC, standard, header comments, design docs | `if`-return, `assert`, length parameter, allocation size | macros, `#ifdef` builds, the caller, a wrapper | checked in every build configuration, not just the one you read |
| Services | API spec, OpenAPI, design docs, README guarantees | middleware, decorator, validation schema, DB constraint | the framework's route registration, not the handler | every route on that path checked, plus the DB schema |
| Firmware / decompiled | datasheet, protocol spec, vendor docs | a compare-and-branch, often unnamed | anywhere; symbol names are absent or wrong | the coverage record says which handlers were read at all |

## Smart contracts

The original target of this plugin. Enforcement is usually a `require` or a custom error, and the trap is that
it delegates: `require(_check(x))` is only enforcement if `_check` compares `x` against the bound the document
names, on the path taken. Follow it.

`unchecked` blocks and assembly suspend guarantees the surrounding code is written as though it still has. A
document requiring that a balance never go below a floor is contradicted by an `unchecked` subtraction even
though a checked one would satisfy it, and the call site looks identical.

Requirements about who may act map to modifiers, `msg.sender` comparisons, and role registries — and to the
constructor and upgrade path, because a document saying the operator cannot reduce a balance is contradicted by
any admin function that can, including one that only moves balances around. Requirements about ordering map to
where state writes sit relative to external calls: "must settle before notifying" is a line-order question.

Watch for arithmetic stated as a percentage and implemented as a numerator. `amountIn * 997 / 1000` satisfies a
0.3% fee and matches nothing you can grep for; verify the arithmetic rather than the wording, and record the
equivalence in the analysis so the next reader does not redo it.

## C and C++

Requirements are usually about bounds, lifetimes, and integer width, and the specification is often an RFC or a
standard rather than a project document — in which case the requirement is normative text with its own section
numbers, and "the code implements RFC 9110 §8.6" is a set of checkable claims rather than one.

The out-parameter is the classic trap: the caller checks the return code and uses the out-parameter, and one
path through the callee returns success without writing it. A requirement that a length is validated is
`partial` if one early return skips the validation.

Check every build configuration. A bound enforced inside `#ifdef DEBUG` is not enforced in the shipped binary,
and a requirement satisfied only under one set of flags should say which. Note the macros — enforcement written
as a macro will not match a search for a function call.

## Services

Authorization and input validation carry most of the requirements, and enforcement usually is not in the handler
body. It is a middleware chain, a decorator, a route registration, or a validation schema declared elsewhere. A
requirement looks `absent` from the handler and is enforced framework-side; a requirement looks satisfied
because one route registers the middleware and three others do not.

So the unit of checking is the route table, not the function. For any requirement about who may call what,
enumerate every registered route on that path and say which ones get the check.

Database constraints are enforcement too. A uniqueness requirement may live in a migration rather than in code,
and a requirement about consistency across two operations is about transactions.

## Firmware and decompiled binaries

Names are absent or wrong, so the rule against inferring behavior from a name is not a caution here — it is the
default condition. Enforcement is a compare-and-branch with no identifier attached to it, and the requirement
has to be recognized from the arithmetic.

Most callees are black boxes and that is normal rather than exceptional. A bound never established in the
visible listing is `absent` with the searches recorded, and that is a complete answer.

Keep a coverage record: which handlers and task entries were read at all. Without it there is no way to
distinguish a requirement that is genuinely unenforced from one enforced in a subsystem nobody opened, and
`absent` cannot be credible.

## When the specification is a standard

RFCs, FIPS documents, and IEEE standards differ from a project whitepaper in two ways that matter.

They are large, so scope the check: name the sections in play and say which were not checked, rather than
implying the whole standard was covered. And they distinguish MUST from SHOULD from MAY deliberately, so the
`force` field carries real weight — a SHOULD the code omits is a documented deviation, not a defect, and
reporting it as one costs credibility on the MUSTs.

They also define terms precisely, and the definition is usually in a different section from the requirement.
Read it before deciding what the requirement demands.

# Worked Examples

Three requirements against real code shapes, one per verdict that is easy to get wrong. Read these for
calibration on how far to chase a requirement before deciding, not as a template to fill in.

---

## `implemented` — arithmetic that satisfies a requirement it does not resemble

> "The protocol charges a fixed 0.3% fee on the input amount for every swap."
> — Whitepaper §4.2

```solidity
// Router.sol:L108
uint256 amountInWithFee = amountIn * 997;
// Router.sol:L110-L111
amountOut = (amountInWithFee * reserveOut) / (reserveIn * 1000 + amountInWithFee);
```

Nothing here contains `fee`, `0.3`, or `30`. Searching the document's vocabulary finds the comment and stops.

The verdict rests on the arithmetic: the input is scaled by 997 and the denominator by 1000, so the fee is
`3/1000 = 0.3%`. Then three things decide whether it is `implemented` rather than `partial`. It is applied
before the output is computed, so it cannot be bypassed by the caller. It is a literal rather than a storage
read, so no admin path changes it. And there is no branch around it — every swap path passes through L108.

Record the equivalence in the analysis. The next reader should not have to rederive that 997/1000 is 0.3%, and
a divergence found later in the same formula will be checked against this note.

**The mistake to avoid:** reporting this as `undecidable` or `absent` because the fee is not named. Verify
arithmetic as arithmetic.

---

## `absent` — the searches are the finding

> "All swap operations MUST enforce a maximum slippage of 1% between expected and actual output."
> — Whitepaper §4.1

```solidity
// RouterV1.sol:L45
function swap(address tokenIn, address tokenOut, uint256 amountIn) external
```

The signature carries no `minAmountOut`, so there is nothing for the caller to express a tolerance with. That
observation alone is suggestive, not conclusive — enforcement could compute the bound internally from an oracle.

What makes the verdict credible is the record:

- `slippage` → 0 hits in `RouterV1.sol`
- `minAmount`, `minOut`, `limitPrice`, `maxDelta` → 0 hits (the document's word is not the code's word, so the
  synonyms are checked too)
- `require`, `revert` in `swap` → 2 hits, both at L47-L48 on `amountIn > 0` and `tokenIn != tokenOut`
- modifiers on `swap` → `nonReentrant` only
- oracle or TWAP reads → none in the file
- `calculateSwapOutput` (the one callee) → read in full; computes output, enforces nothing
- callers of `swap` → none in scope; it is an entrypoint

Six places it could have been, none of them holding it. That is an absence. Without the list it is a guess in
citation format.

**The mistake to avoid:** concluding `absent` after searching only the document's own vocabulary.

---

## `partial` — enforcement that exists on the path nobody tested

> "The parser MUST reject any frame whose declared length exceeds the remaining buffer."
> — RFC §4.3

```c
/* proto.c:L112-L124 */
int parse_frame(const uint8_t *buf, size_t len, frame_t *out) {
    if (len < HDR) return -1;

     4	/// @title raffle.fun Raffle Factory Interface
     5	/// @author heesho
     6	/// @notice Defines atomic ERC-1167 raffle creation for one immutable USDC, treasury, and Chainlink configuration.
     7	/// @dev The factory has no owner, pause, upgrade, rescue, or mutable protocol configuration. Deployment tooling must
     8	///      verify that the immutable quote-token address is the target chain's official USDC; onchain construction checks
     9	///      only code presence and six-decimal metadata.
    10	/// @custom:version 1.0.0
    11	interface IRaffleFactory {
    12	    // Types
    13	
    14	    /// @notice Sponsor-selected configuration for one new raffle.
    15	    /// @param sponsorRecipient Immutable recipient of sponsor quote proceeds and any returned prize.
    16	    /// @param prizeToken Standards-compliant ERC-721 prize contract.
    17	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID to escrow atomically during creation.
    18	    /// @param reserveEntries Global raw entry-count threshold selecting the NFT outcome when met or exceeded.
    19	    /// @param endTime Exclusive sale-end Unix timestamp, in seconds.
    20	    struct CreateRaffleParams {
    21	        address sponsorRecipient;
    22	        address prizeToken;
    23	        uint256 prizeTokenId;
    24	        uint128 reserveEntries;
    25	        uint64 endTime;
    26	    }
    27	
    28	    // Events
    29	
    30	    /// @notice Emitted after a raffle clone is initialized, registered, funded, and active.
    31	    /// @param raffleId One-based canonical raffle identifier.
    32	    /// @param raffle Newly created fixed-target ERC-1167 clone.
    33	    /// @param sponsor Prize depositor and pre-end empty-raffle refund authority.
    34	    /// @param sponsorRecipient Immutable recipient of sponsor quote proceeds and any returned prize.
    35	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 contract of the escrowed prize.
    36	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID of the escrowed prize.
    37	    /// @param quoteToken Immutable canonical six-decimal USDC contract used by the raffle.
    38	    /// @param protocolTreasury Immutable recipient of protocol fees.
    39	    /// @param reserveEntries Global raw entry-count threshold selecting the NFT outcome when met or exceeded.
    40	    /// @param endTime Exclusive sale-end Unix timestamp, in seconds.
    41	    event RaffleCreated(
    42	        uint256 indexed raffleId,
    43	        address indexed raffle,
    44	        address indexed sponsor,
    45	        address sponsorRecipient,
    46	        address prizeToken,
    47	        uint256 prizeTokenId,
    48	        address quoteToken,
    49	        address protocolTreasury,
    50	        uint128 reserveEntries,
    51	        uint64 endTime
    52	    );
    53	
    54	    // Errors
    55	
    56	    /// @notice Raised when a required address is the zero address.
    57	    error ZeroAddress();
    58	
    59	    /// @notice Raised when an address required to contain deployed code is not a contract.
    60	    /// @param account Address whose code length was zero.
    61	    error NotContract(address account);
    62	
    63	    /// @notice Raised when the quote token cannot report its decimal precision.
    64	    /// @param quoteToken Rejected quote-token contract.
    65	    error UnsupportedQuoteToken(address quoteToken);
    66	
    67	    /// @notice Raised when the quote token does not use the required six-decimal precision.
    68	    /// @param actualDecimals Decimal precision reported by the quote token.
    69	    /// @param requiredDecimals Required decimal precision, exactly six.
    70	    error InvalidQuoteTokenDecimals(uint8 actualDecimals, uint8 requiredDecimals);
    71	
    72	    /// @notice Raised when the prize contract does not report ERC-721 interface support.
    73	    /// @param prizeToken Rejected prize-token contract.
    74	    error UnsupportedPrizeToken(address prizeToken);
    75	
    76	    /// @notice Raised when a raffle is configured with a zero reserve entry threshold.
    77	    error ZeroReserveEntries();
    78	
    79	    /// @notice Raised when the sale end is not strictly after the creation block timestamp.
    80	    /// @param currentTime Current block Unix timestamp, in seconds.
    81	    /// @param endTime Supplied exclusive sale-end Unix timestamp, in seconds.
    82	    error InvalidEndTime(uint256 currentTime, uint256 endTime);
    83	
    84	    /// @notice Raised when the prospective sale duration exceeds the fixed 30-day limit.
    85	    /// @param duration Prospective sale duration in seconds.
    86	    /// @param maximumDuration Maximum permitted sale duration in seconds.
    87	    error SaleDurationTooLong(uint256 duration, uint256 maximumDuration);
    88	
    89	    /// @notice Raised when a configured token or recipient is known protocol plumbing.
    90	    /// @param destination Rejected address.
    91	    error UnsafeProtocolDestination(address destination);
    92	
    93	    /// @notice Raised when the exact configured prize is not owned by an active clone after escrow.
    94	    /// @param raffle Newly created clone expected to hold the prize and report `Active`.
    95	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 prize contract.
    96	    /// @param prizeTokenId Configured prize token ID.
    97	    error PrizeEscrowVerificationFailed(address raffle, address prizeToken, uint256 prizeTokenId);
    98	
    99	    // External state-changing functions
   100	
   101	    /// @notice Creates, initializes, registers, and funds one autonomous fixed-target raffle clone atomically.
   102	    /// @param params Sponsor-selected recipient, prize, reserve, and timing configuration.
   103	    /// @return raffle Address of the newly created and activated clone.
   104	    function createRaffle(CreateRaffleParams calldata params) external returns (address raffle);
   105	
   106	    // Public generated getters
   107	
   108	    /// @notice Returns the immutable canonical six-decimal USDC contract used by every raffle.
   109	    /// @return quoteTokenAddress Canonical USDC contract address trusted by this deployment.
   110	    function quoteToken() external view returns (address quoteTokenAddress);
   111	
   112	    /// @notice Returns the immutable Chainlink VRF v2.5 native direct-funding wrapper used by every raffle.
   113	    /// @return wrapperAddress Wrapper contract address.
   114	    function vrfWrapper() external view returns (address wrapperAddress);
   115	
   116	    /// @notice Returns the immutable recipient of protocol fees from every raffle.
   117	    /// @return treasuryAddress Protocol treasury address.
   118	    function protocolTreasury() external view returns (address treasuryAddress);
   119	
   120	    /// @notice Returns the fixed Chainlink callback execution limit used by every raffle.
   121	    /// @return gasLimit Callback gas units requested from the wrapper.
   122	    function callbackGasLimit() external view returns (uint32 gasLimit);
   123	
   124	    /// @notice Returns the fixed Chainlink confirmation count used by every raffle.
   125	    /// @return confirmations Blocks requested before callback fulfillment.
   126	    function requestConfirmations() external view returns (uint16 confirmations);
   127	
   128	    /// @notice Returns the immutable implementation targeted by every registered ERC-1167 clone.
   129	    /// @return implementation Locked raffle implementation address.
   130	    function raffleImplementation() external view returns (address implementation);
   131	
   132	    /// @notice Returns the lifetime number of successfully created raffles.
   133	    /// @return count Latest one-based raffle identifier and total registered raffle count.
   134	    function raffleCount() external view returns (uint256 count);
   135	
   136	    /// @notice Returns whether an address is a raffle registered by this factory.
   137	    /// @param raffle Address to check.
   138	    /// @return registered True only for a successfully created canonical clone.
   139	    function isRaffle(address raffle) external view returns (bool registered);
   140	
   141	    /// @notice Returns the canonical raffle address for an identifier.
   142	    /// @param raffleId One-based raffle identifier.
   143	    /// @return raffle Registered clone address, or the zero address for an unknown identifier.
   144	    function raffleById(uint256 raffleId) external view returns (address raffle);
   145	
   146	    /// @notice Returns the canonical identifier assigned to a raffle address.
   147	    /// @param raffle Address to query.
   148	    /// @return raffleId One-based identifier, or zero for an unregistered address.
   149	    function idByRaffle(address raffle) external view returns (uint256 raffleId);
   150	}

     4	import { IVRFV2PlusWrapper } from "@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/vrf/dev/interfaces/IVRFV2PlusWrapper.sol";
     5	import { IERC20 } from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol";
     6	import { IERC721 } from "@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721.sol";

     8	/// @title raffle.fun Raffle Interface
     9	/// @author heesho
    10	/// @notice Defines one autonomous NFT raffle using fixed-price USDC entries and one transferable ERC-721 ticket per
    11	///         purchase.
    12	/// @dev Ticket IDs are sequential. Each ticket stores one inclusive uint128 entry range and remains a transferable
    13	///      bearer claim until its owner atomically burns it for redemption or refund. The immutable quote token is trusted
    14	///      canonical six-decimal USDC with standard, non-rebasing, fee-free transfers. Supported prizes are honest,
    15	///      standards-compliant ERC-721s.
    16	/// @custom:version 1.0.0
    17	interface IRaffle {
    18	    // Types
    19	
    20	    /// @notice The single authoritative raffle lifecycle and economic result.
    21	    enum Status {
    22	        /// @notice The clone is initialized and waiting for the factory to escrow the configured prize.
    23	        AwaitingPrize,
    24	        /// @notice The prize is escrowed and entry sales or post-sale draw initiation are available.
    25	        Active,
    26	        /// @notice A Chainlink VRF request was accepted and its callback window is open.
    27	        Drawing,
    28	        /// @notice The reserve was met and the winning ticket may redeem the prize NFT.
    29	        NftWon,
    30	        /// @notice The reserve was missed and the winning ticket may redeem its cash allocation.
    31	        CashWon,
    32	        /// @notice Full ticket refunds are enabled and the sponsor may recover the prize NFT.
    33	        Refunding
    34	    }
    35	
    36	    /// @notice Complete clone-specific configuration supplied once by the canonical factory.
    37	    /// @param sponsor Prize depositor and empty-raffle cancellation authority.
    38	    /// @param sponsorRecipient Immutable recipient of sponsor quote proceeds and any returned prize.
    39	    /// @param protocolTreasury Immutable recipient of protocol fees.
    40	    /// @param prizeToken Standards-compliant ERC-721 prize contract.
    41	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID of the prize escrowed by this raffle.
    42	    /// @param raffleId One-based canonical factory identifier for this raffle.
    43	    /// @param reserveEntries Global raw entry-count threshold selecting the NFT outcome when met or exceeded.
    44	    /// @param endTime Unix timestamp, in seconds, at which entry sales end exclusively.
    45	    struct RaffleInitParams {
    46	        address sponsor;
    47	        address sponsorRecipient;
    48	        address protocolTreasury;
    49	        address prizeToken;
    50	        uint256 prizeTokenId;
    51	        uint256 raffleId;
    52	        uint128 reserveEntries;
    53	        uint64 endTime;
    54	    }
    55	
    56	    // Events
    57	
    58	    /// @notice Emitted when the factory deposits the configured prize and activates the raffle.
    59	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 contract of the deposited prize.
    60	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID of the deposited prize.
    61	    /// @param sponsor Address that deposited the prize through the factory.
    62	    event PrizeDeposited(address indexed prizeToken, uint256 indexed prizeTokenId, address indexed sponsor);
    63	
    64	    /// @notice Emitted when a buyer pays for entries and one range ticket is minted.
    65	    /// @param buyer Address that paid the six-decimal quote-token amount.
    66	    /// @param recipient Address that received the newly minted ticket.
    67	    /// @param ticketId Sequential ticket ID assigned to the purchase.
    68	    /// @param firstEntry First global raffle entry represented by the ticket, inclusive.
    69	    /// @param lastEntry Last global raffle entry represented by the ticket, inclusive.
    70	    /// @param entryCount Number of entries represented by the ticket.
    71	    /// @param grossAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid, equal to `entryCount * ENTRY_PRICE`.
    72	    event TicketPurchased(
    73	        address indexed buyer,
    74	        address indexed recipient,
    75	        uint256 indexed ticketId,
    76	        uint128 firstEntry,
    77	        uint128 lastEntry,
    78	        uint128 entryCount,
    79	        uint256 grossAmount
    80	    );
    81	
    82	    /// @notice Emitted when the raffle pays for and records its one Chainlink VRF request.
    83	    /// @param requestId Wrapper-assigned request identifier.
    84	    /// @param requester Address that initiated and funded the request.
    85	    /// @param fee Native-token wei actually paid to the wrapper for the request.
    86	    /// @param excessReturned Native-token wei returned to the requester after paying the actual fee.
    87	    /// @param drawRequestedAt Unix timestamp, in seconds, when the request was accepted.
    88	    /// @param callbackDeadline Exclusive Unix-timestamp deadline for accepting the authenticated callback.
    89	    event DrawRequested(
    90	        uint256 indexed requestId,
    91	        address indexed requester,
    92	        uint256 fee,
    93	        uint256 excessReturned,
    94	        uint256 drawRequestedAt,
    95	        uint256 callbackDeadline
    96	    );
    97	
    98	    /// @notice Emitted when an authenticated, ABI-decodable callback cannot resolve the raffle.
    99	    /// @param receivedRequestId Request ID supplied by the wrapper callback.
   100	    /// @param expectedRequestId Request ID currently recorded by the raffle, or zero before request persistence.
   101	    /// @param status Current raffle status when the callback is ignored.
   102	    event VrfCallbackIgnored(uint256 indexed receivedRequestId, uint256 indexed expectedRequestId, Status status);
   103	
   104	    /// @notice Emitted when an authenticated callback selects the winning entry and final result.
   105	    /// @param requestId Request ID that produced the accepted randomness.
   106	    /// @param winningEntry Selected one-based global entry number in `[1,totalEntries]`.
   107	    /// @param result Final `NftWon` or `CashWon` result.
   108	    event RaffleResolved(uint256 indexed requestId, uint128 indexed winningEntry, Status indexed result);
   109	
   110	    /// @notice Emitted when the raffle enters the full-refund branch.
   111	    /// @param finalizer Address that enabled refunds.
   112	    /// @param remainingRefundLiability Raw six-decimal quote-token units initially available for ticket refunds.
   113	    event RefundsEnabled(address indexed finalizer, uint256 remainingRefundLiability);
   114	
   115	    /// @notice Emitted when the winning ticket is proven and all terminal quote-token liabilities are allocated.
   116	    /// @param ticketId Ticket proven to contain the selected winning entry.
   117	    /// @param settler Address that performed permissionless settlement.
   118	    /// @param result Final `NftWon` or `CashWon` result.
   119	    /// @param cashAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units allocated to the cash winner; zero for `NftWon`.
   120	    /// @param protocolFee Raw six-decimal quote-token units allocated to the treasury, rounded down from gross sales.
   121	    /// @param sponsorAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units allocated to the sponsor recipient as the remainder.
   122	    event WinningTicketSettled(
   123	        uint256 indexed ticketId,
   124	        address indexed settler,
   125	        Status indexed result,
   126	        uint256 cashAmount,
   127	        uint256 protocolFee,
   128	        uint256 sponsorAmount
   129	    );
   130	
   131	    /// @notice Emitted when the winning ticket owner burns the ticket and receives the corresponding prize.
   132	    /// @param ticketId Burned winning ticket ID.
   133	    /// @param winner Ticket owner that received the prize at redemption time.
   134	    /// @param result Final `NftWon` or `CashWon` result.
   135	    /// @param cashAmount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid for `CashWon`; zero for `NftWon`.
   136	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 prize contract for `NftWon`; the zero address for `CashWon`.
   137	    /// @param prizeTokenId ERC-721 prize token ID for `NftWon`; zero for `CashWon`.
   138	    event WinningTicketRedeemed(
   139	        uint256 indexed ticketId,
   140	        address indexed winner,
   141	        Status indexed result,
   142	        uint256 cashAmount,
   143	        address prizeToken,
   144	        uint256 prizeTokenId
   145	    );
   146	
   147	    /// @notice Emitted when an owner burns one or more tickets for a full quote-token refund.
   148	    /// @param owner Ticket owner that burned the tickets and received the refund.
   149	    /// @param ticketQuantity Number of tickets burned in this transaction.
   150	    /// @param entryQuantity Aggregate number of entries represented by the burned tickets.
   151	    /// @param amount Raw six-decimal quote-token units refunded, equal to `entryQuantity * ENTRY_PRICE`.
   152	    /// @param remainingRefundLiability Raw six-decimal quote-token units still claimable after this refund.
   153	    event TicketsRefunded(
   154	        address indexed owner,
   155	        uint256 ticketQuantity,
   156	        uint256 entryQuantity,
   157	        uint256 amount,
   158	        uint256 remainingRefundLiability
   159	    );
   160	
   161	    /// @notice Emitted when the complete current sponsor balance is released to its immutable recipient.
   162	    /// @param caller Address that triggered the permissionless release.
   163	    /// @param recipient Immutable sponsor recipient that received the payment.
   164	    /// @param amount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid.
   165	    event SponsorProceedsReleased(address indexed caller, address indexed recipient, uint256 amount);
   166	
   167	    /// @notice Emitted when the complete current protocol-fee balance is released to the immutable treasury.
   168	    /// @param caller Address that triggered the permissionless release.
   169	    /// @param treasury Immutable protocol treasury that received the payment.
   170	    /// @param amount Raw six-decimal quote-token units paid.
   171	    event ProtocolFeesReleased(address indexed caller, address indexed treasury, uint256 amount);
   172	
   173	    /// @notice Emitted when the escrowed prize is returned after a cash result or refund transition.
   174	    /// @param caller Address that triggered the permissionless release.
   175	    /// @param recipient Immutable sponsor recipient that received the prize.
   176	    /// @param prizeToken ERC-721 contract of the returned prize.
   177	    /// @param prizeTokenId Token ID of the returned prize.
   178	    event SponsorPrizeReleased(
   179	        address indexed caller, address indexed recipient, address indexed prizeToken, uint256 prizeTokenId
   180	    );
   181	
   182	    // Errors
   183	
   184	    /// @notice Raised when a caller other than the immutable factory attempts clone initialization.
   185	    error OnlyFactory();
   186	
   187	    /// @notice Raised when initialization is attempted more than once or on the locked implementation.
   188	    error AlreadyInitialized();
   189	
   190	    /// @notice Raised when a required address is the zero address.
   191	    error ZeroAddress();
   192	
   193	    /// @notice Raised when an operation is unavailable in the current lifecycle state.
   194	    /// @param actual Current raffle status.
   195	    error InvalidStatus(Status actual);
   196	
   197	    /// @notice Raised when an ERC-721 receiver callback does not exactly match the configured factory prize deposit.
   198	    /// @param token ERC-721 contract that invoked the receiver callback.
   199	    /// @param tokenId Token ID supplied by the callback.
   200	    /// @param from Address identified as the previous token owner.
   201	    /// @param operator Address identified as the transfer operator.
   202	    error UnexpectedPrize(address token, uint256 tokenId, address from, address operator);
   203	
   204	    /// @notice Raised when an entry purchase is submitted at or after the exclusive sale end.
   205	    /// @param endTime Exclusive sale-end Unix timestamp, in seconds.
   206	    /// @param currentTime Current block Unix timestamp, in seconds.
   207	    error SaleEnded(uint256 endTime, uint256 currentTime);
   208	
   209	    /// @notice Raised when an entry ticket would be minted to the zero address.
   210	    error InvalidRecipient();
   211	
   212	    /// @notice Raised when a purchase requests no entries.
   213	    error ZeroEntryCount();
   214

### U-01 — Zero reserves and sales longer than 30 days are rejected

Factory validation rejects reserveEntries == 0, and createRaffle rejects a prospective sale duration above 30 days (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L97-L104,L154-L179; packages/contracts/src/libraries/RaffleConstants.sol:L29-L30). ### U-02 — The depositor can nominate a different permanent beneficiary

createRaffle records msg.sender as sponsor while accepting a separate sponsorRecipient; proceeds and every returned prize go to the latter (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L97-L120,L154-L169; packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L197-L204,L375-L405). A sponsor chooses this routing at creation, after which no recipient setter exists in the supplied configuration path. DESIGN.md says “95% sponsor,” “15% sponsor,” “Refund outcome ... returns prize,” and “Sponsor and treasury can claim independently” without introducing a separate beneficiary role (DESIGN.md:L2).

### U-03 — Ticket recipients are denied beyond the stated cross-clone rule

Every ticket mint and transfer rejects the raffle itself, factory, quote token, wrapper, configured prize token, implementation, and a currently registered same-factory raffle (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L491-L502,L587-L604). Buyers reach the rule by choosing a mint recipient; owners or approved operators reach it through inherited ERC-721 transfers (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L209-L235; packages/contracts/node_modules/@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol:L115-L135). DESIGN.md promises “a transferable ERC721 ticket” and says “Never move assets between raffle clones,” but does not disclose the additional prohibited recipient classes (DESIGN.md:L2).

### U-04 — Draw requests are caller-funded native-token operations with fixed parameters and an atomic excess refund

Direct native transfers revert; requestDraw asks for one word with a 300,000 callback-gas limit and 30 confirmations, pays the wrapper, and sends excess native value back to msg.sender. A requester that cannot accept the excess causes the request transaction to revert (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L43-L50,L170-L173,L240-L272; packages/contracts/src/libraries/RaffleConstants.sol:L38-L42; packages/contracts/node_modules/@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/vrf/dev/VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol:L76-L88). Any address can reach this path after the sale under the request-state conditions. DESIGN.md states only “Request window [sale end, end+2days)” and “Quote token and Chainlink wrapper are trusted canonical dependencies”; it does not specify the funder, native payment, one-word request, fixed gas/confirmation values, or refund callback (DESIGN.md:L2).

After wrapper authentication, a synchronous, wrong-state, wrong-ID, wrong-length, or late ABI-decodable callback emits VrfCallbackIgnored and returns normally without changing the result (packages/contracts/node_modules/@chainlink/contracts/src/v0.8/vrf/dev/VRFV2PlusWrapperConsumerBase.sol:L99-L107; packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L504-L516). Only the configured wrapper can reach this behavior. DESIGN.md states “callback accepted strictly before request timestamp+2days” and “Callback records result only,” but does not say rejected authenticated callbacks return successfully or emit an acknowledgement (DESIGN.md:L2).

An accepted callback maps its sole word to (randomWords[0] % totalEntries) + 1 (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L509-L523). The configured wrapper reaches this operation with a timely matching callback. DESIGN.md says “Callback records result only” but gives no randomness-to-entry mapping, so a reader cannot reproduce the winning entry from the design alone (DESIGN.md:L2).

That state permits the prize-return path (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L395-L405). DESIGN.md says “Refunds open at deadline” and does not disclose this sponsor-only pre-deadline branch (DESIGN.md:L2). This is also the behavioral divergence reported as F-03 / REQ-35.

refundTickets rejects an empty list and any list longer than MAX_REFUND_TICKET_BATCH_SIZE, which is 100 (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L348-L369; packages/contracts/src/libraries/RaffleConstants.sol:L26-L27). ### F-01 — Untrusted prize self-reports stand in for escrow and delivery

**Severity: Critical. Behavioral/security consequence.**

Surviving requirements:

- **REQ-14:** “Exactly one ERC721 prize is escrowed atomically at creation.” — DESIGN.md:L2
- **REQ-48:** “Quote token and Chainlink wrapper are trusted canonical dependencies; arbitrary prize contracts and ticket recipients are untrusted.” — DESIGN.md:L2
- **REQ-53:** “Quote token and Chainlink wrapper are trusted canonical dependencies; arbitrary prize contracts and ticket recipients are untrusted.” — DESIGN.md:L2

**What the code does instead.** Creation accepts any code-bearing sponsor-selected prize contract that returns true for its own ERC-165 query (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L154-L177). The same selected contract executes safeTransferFrom and supplies the ownerOf answer used as the factory's custody postcondition (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L127-L134). The raffle becomes Active when that contract calls the public receiver with the expected tuple; the receiver validates the caller and arguments but has no ownership fact independent of the caller (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L416-L430). Inline production documentation makes the dependency explicit by stating, “Supported prizes are honest, standards-compliant ERC-721s” (packages/contracts/src/interfaces/IRaffle.sol:L12-L15), which conflicts with DESIGN.md's verbatim “arbitrary prize contracts ... are untrusted” boundary.

The dependency persists after resolution. NftWon settlement allocates the gross quote-token pot into sponsor and protocol liabilities without touching the prize (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L533-L555), and those liabilities may be released in separate transactions without a winner-redemption or prize-delivery condition (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L375-L391). Winner redemption then calls the arbitrary prize's transferFrom and trusts that same contract's ownerOf report (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L329-L337).

**Reachability and consequence.**

1. An external sponsor selects a contract that reports ERC-721 support, invokes the raffle receiver with the accepted fields, and reports the new raffle as owner. Those are sufficient for createRaffle to publish the raffle as active (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L97-L147; packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L421-L430).
2. Entrants can then pay the immutable quote token; each purchase adds entryCount × 1,000,000 units to unsettledPot (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L209-L235; packages/contracts/src/libraries/RaffleConstants.sol:L20-L24).
3. A timely authenticated callback can select NftWon, after which permissionless settlement records sponsor and treasury claims and their release functions can complete (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L509-L523,L533-L557,L375-L391).
4. The prize contract can later revert on transfer, leaving the winner unable to complete redemption after earlier payout transactions have finalized, or it can return from transferFrom and report the winner from ownerOf without an independently established NFT ownership transition (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L323-L337). Reversion rolls back only that redemption transaction; it does not reverse earlier settlement or release transactions.

The demonstrated consequence is therefore not merely interface nonconformance: buyer-funded quote-token liabilities can be allocated and released although the target has no enforceable fact that one NFT was escrowed or delivered. An actor expressly outside the documented trust boundary chooses this path, so value can move under conditions DESIGN.md rules out. That makes the finding Critical under the consequence rubric. REQ-14, REQ-48, and REQ-53 are three views of this same root cause and are intentionally not counted as separate findings.

### F-02 — A future clone address defeats destination invariants

**Severity: High. Behavioral/security consequence.**

Surviving requirements:

- **REQ-44:** “Sponsor and treasury can claim independently after settlement.” — DESIGN.md:L2
- **REQ-47:** “Never move assets between raffle clones.” — DESIGN.md:L2

**What the code does instead.** Creation rejects a sponsor recipient only if it is already known as protocol plumbing or is already registered as a raffle (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L154-L169). The factory later deploys clones with ordinary CREATE and registers their addresses (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L105-L125; packages/contracts/node_modules/@openzeppelin/contracts/proxy/Clones.sol:L24-L60). The raffle's runtime classifier treats a code-bearing address as unsafe when the factory now reports it as a raffle (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L593-L604).

The two asset paths then disagree:

- Sponsor quote proceeds pass through a fresh destination check, so releaseSponsorProceeds reverts after the stored recipient becomes a registered clone (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L375-L380,L564-L566,L598-L604).
- Sponsor-prize return reads the same stored recipient but performs no fresh destination check and calls unsafe ERC-721 transferFrom (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L395-L405). transferFrom does not invoke ERC721 receiver acceptance; only safeTransferFrom adds that callback (packages/contracts/node_modules/@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol:L115-L135; packages/contracts/node_modules/@openzeppelin/contracts/token/ERC721/IERC721.sol:L75-L91).

**Reachability and consequence.** A sponsor can choose the predictable, presently code-less address of a future same-factory CREATE clone as raffle A's sponsorRecipient. It passes both current-state checks and is stored (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L154-L169; packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L181-L205,L593-L604). A later successful creation deploys and registers clone B at that address (packages/contracts/src/RaffleFactory.sol:L105-L125; packages/contracts/node_modules/@openzeppelin/contracts/proxy/Clones.sol:L47-L60).

Afterward, A's sponsor proceeds cannot be released because B is now rejected at transfer time, leaving the allocated sponsor bucket in A while the treasury's separate bucket remains callable (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L375-L391,L551-L555,L564-L566). On the prize-return path, however, A sends its prize directly to B without reclassification or a receiver callback (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L395-L405). The NFT is then outside B's raffle accounting, and the source says unrelated NFTs received through unsafe transferFrom cannot be rescued (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L409-L411).

This needs unusual but source-reachable nonce/address coordination, and the actor chooses the affected recipient. Those gates keep it below Critical. Enforcement exists on the ordinary paths yet fails on one reachable asset path, and the outcome includes both a blocked entitlement and an actual cross-clone NFT transfer, so High is consequence-proportionate. REQ-44 and REQ-47 are cross-linked here because both arise from the same time-of-check/time-of-use address classification.

### F-03 — The sponsor can close an empty raffle before its deadline

**Severity: Medium. Behavioral consequence with bounded reach.**

Surviving requirement:

- **REQ-35:** “Refunds open at deadline.” — DESIGN.md:L2

**What the code does instead.** Sold Active raffles reject refunds before endTime + 2 days, and Drawing raffles reject refunds before drawRequestedAt + 2 days; equality is accepted on both paths (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L285-L300,L458-L465; packages/contracts/src/libraries/RaffleConstants.sol:L32-L36). But on a zero-entry Active raffle, the only pre-endTime check is conditioned on msg.sender != sponsor. The sponsor therefore bypasses the assigned deadline, sets the same Refunding status, and can then release the prize (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L279-L300,L395-L405).

**Reachability and consequence.** Every newly activated raffle begins with zero entries because initialization does not add entries and purchases are the only positive totalEntries writer (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L176-L205,L223-L233). The sponsor can call enableRefunds before endTime, permanently close that raffle, and return the escrowed prize to sponsorRecipient (packages/contracts/src/Raffle.sol:L276-L300,L395-L406). No ticket owner loses a refund on this path because the branch requires zero sold entries. The established consequence is an early sponsor-controlled cancellation of an advertised raffle and early prize return; any wider reliance by prospective entrants was not established in source. The privilege, zero-entry condition, and bounded consequence make this Medium rather than High.
